exploit_narrative: The expert is likely over-indexing on missing evidence in a helper file and underestimating the chance that this is not the real trust boundary at all. From an attacker perspective, the interesting question is whether `runtime-sdk-macros/src/generators.rs` emits ingress wrappers or only generic token plumbing. The visible snippet strongly suggests the latter: `wrap_in_const` is scope hygiene, and `sdk_crate_path()` is crate-resolution support. Neither is a natural place to enforce caller binding, authorization, or boundary revalidation. So the claimed issue may be a boundary-mapping error rather than a missing-control bug. That said, macros are dangerous exactly because security-critical logic can be hidden in generated code. If this file also contains generator routines that expand dispatch/entry wrappers, a subtle omission could systematically affect every runtime method: generated entrypoints might deserialize external input and dispatch directly into privileged handlers without re-checking origin, call format, or fail-closed semantics. In that scenario, exploitation would be broad and architectural, because developers would trust the macro to synthesize safe ingress code. But based on the provided snippet alone, an attacker cannot yet point to an actual exploit path; the stronger attack is on the review assumption that this file is the enforcement point.
counter_arguments: The provided code is plainly utility-level macro support, not direct runtime ingress handling.
Absence of visible checks in helper functions is not evidence that generated entry wrappers omit those checks.
Authorization and caller binding may be enforced in the runtime core after macro-generated dispatch, making this file boundary-adjacent rather than boundary-owning.
Trust-boundary obligations in TEE systems are often split across layers: host call decoding, transaction/check layer, dispatcher, and method context construction.
A proc-macro crate cannot itself execute runtime policy; it only emits code, so the real question is what expansions are produced at call sites, which is not shown.
The tool hits around `enum_binding` and `match #enum_binding` hint at enum dispatch generation, but dispatch matching alone does not imply a missing security check.
If generated methods receive a pre-validated context object from lower layers, caller binding may already be established before any macro-emitted code runs.
The case may be mislabeled because the selected file appears to contain generic generators rather than the runtime-facing boundary implementation.
